Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen, and it's my pleasure to welcome you to this press briefing of the first working day of Denmark's presidency of the Security Council for the month of August. My name is Emil Poulsen. I'm the spokesperson of the Permanent Mission of Denmark to the United Nations. And let me also start by paying tribute to the Permanent Mission of the Democratic Republic of Congo for their stewardship of the work of the Security Council for July. It's an honour for Denmark to assume the responsibility for August. I'm especially delighted to welcome Her Excellency Ambassador Christina Markus-Lassen, our Permanent Representative to the United Nations, who shortly will present the programme of work of the Security Council for August. She's accompanied by our Political Coordinator, Minister-Counsellor Mr. Troels Rappo Bey. Afterwards, we will have a short Q&A session I would kindly plea that you introduce yourself and also indicate which media you represent. I intend to take it in batches of 3 questions at a time. So without further ado, Madam Ambassador, you have the floor.

Thank you so much, Emile, and good afternoon, everyone. Very nice to see you all. I realize this is in the middle of the holiday season and also the weather was awful today, so really thank you for joining us today and thank you for your interest and your continued coverage of of the Council's work. It's very much appreciated. I think you will all agree that Denmark assumes the presidency of the Security Council at a time of deep uncertainty for international peace and security. We see conflicts escalating. We see humanitarian suffering is increasing. Geopolitical tensions are rising. And political solutions seem out of reach in many regions of the world. And on many of the topics that we also discuss in the Council, whether it's Ukraine, Sudan, the Middle East and the Gulf, we do fear further escalation also in light of what we've seen over recent weeks. So any of these topics could, of course, end up on the Council's agenda in the coming months. But I'll start by the programme of work that I think you have also received and which was adopted, of course, right now this morning. You will see that we have not overburdened the agenda. We all say this at presidencies, but we also know that there will be, unfortunately, a lot of extraordinary meetings on the Council agenda, so we are happy to leave space for that, and in particular in the light of some of the ongoing crises that I just mentioned. But we already do have, of course, mandated meetings this month of August on South Sudan, Yemen, Libya, the occupied Palestinian territories, DPRK, Syria, and the fight against terrorism. And through these meetings, as well as the additional meetings that may be added to the calendar, our programme would really span across critical regional and thematic files, and all, of course, in support of our goal to maintain international peace and security. We believe— I hope you agree with us— that Denmark has been a consistent member throughout our term. Consistent in our demands for international law, including international humanitarian law, to be upheld without exception, and consistent in upholding our priorities on women, peace, and security, and climate, peace, and security. And you will also see focus on these issues during our presidency month. So this month, the way we have shaped the program, we hope that it will very much reflect the key issues we've sought to progress as an elected member. It's been a little bit more than a year and a half now. So as our membership throughout our term. So as has also been the case for many months now, you can expect us to seek to bring attention to Sudan and Ukraine, where Council engagement, we believe, remains especially urgent. In Sudan, we'll continue to press for stronger protection of civilians, greater humanitarian access, and renewed efforts towards ending the conflict. And on Ukraine, we'll maintain our call for an immediate and unconditional ceasefire, as well as our constant support for comprehensive, just, and lasting peace in line with the UN Charter, while keeping the consequences of Russia's aggression firmly on the Council's agenda. And I realize you've heard me say this before, but I wanted to still restate it. Across our agenda, we see that where conflicts erupt, hunger often follows. And that's really the background for the so-called signature event that we are hosting under the leadership of the Danish Minister for Foreign Affairs on the 25th of August. It's going to be a high-level open debate on conflict and hunger, an issue again that we have consistently championed. And we want to use this debate to see how the Council can better implement Resolution 2417, which is exactly about this issue. It's a topic that we mean— that we believe is only underscored by the current developments in the Strait of Hormuz, as well as several other of the conflicts— ongoing conflicts we see out there. We have one more open debate, and that's the annual debate on working methods. That's going to be on the 19th of August. That's also, we believe, advancing our longstanding commitment to a more effective, transparent, and inclusive Security Council. So that's really a topic that we believe is very important and also where we want the whole engagement, hopefully, of the wider membership of the UN. Then there are several known unknowns, if I may use that expression, that we can expect, that we can't confirm yet, but we expect this month also. We hope to very soon receive the Secretary-General's review of the future of peace operations. It's been in the works for a while, as you know. So if and when we receive that, we expect together with Pakistan, who's our co-partner in the DUO, Cooperation on the Future of Peace Operations. We hope for Council consultations, at least a discussion of that, to address and assess the report. That's going to be very important. It's something that's been very much in focus also in our membership. So looking forward to that also. I think another thing I didn't mention yet, but which we also would be watching very closely, the situation in the West Bank, but also in Gaza. On the latter, we hope to see, of course, progress on the implementation of 2803, but also on the West Bank. We've seen a lot of concerning incidents over the last few weeks and months, so we could also expect that those two issues might be on the agenda. The same goes for the situation in Lebanon. The post-unifil arrangements will have to be decided, as you know, by the council members. We have been presented by some options by the Secretary General. Right now, we are finding waiting for the best time to. Actually discuss that future configuration. Then August is also a month— this is also not on the programme— it's a very rather grim anniversary, we believe, of the 5 years since Taliban's seizure of power in Afghanistan. And we'll also find some way to mark that occasion so we all have some focus on that and the many consequences it's had for the population, in particular for women and girls. And then finally, I know you're all waiting for it. We do hope, of course, to make progress on the selection of the new Secretary-General. This is arguably one of the most important decisions of the Council this year. We obviously cannot comment on the results, if you wanted to ask me that, of the straw polls last week, but we do expect to conduct another round of straw polls later this month. We are, as presidency right now, aiming for and hoping to schedule on the 21st of August, but obviously, as you can appreciate, there's a lot of bits and pieces out there that are variable, that are moving, so— but that's at least our aim for now with that date, and we assume that there will certainly be one straw poll during our presidency. We see this as a joint process under the Charter, so this will all be done in cooperation with the General Assembly also. As you know, there needs to be also a hearing, an interactive dialogue with the General Assembly. So these are some— I feel that was quite a lot already. These are some of the issues on our mind, our agenda for the coming month. They represent the ones I've mentioned, areas also where we believe that the Council should do more and should act, and at the very least they direct our continued attention. So this is something I can promise you for this month as presidency. continue to work for solutions and also remaining very strong in our principles. That's it for me now, but I will look forward to receiving your questions and comments.

Yeah, I think it's— for us, it is extremely important to shed some light on both how many of these major conflicts, and it's basically all the ones I was talking about right now, Strait of Hormuz, Ukraine, even what's happened in the Palestinian territories, are affecting food security, but at the same time, of course, also sometimes conflicts over food resources will also have the opposite effect or actually spur conflicts. We have some interesting briefers including of course our Secretary-General, and then we'll have, as I mentioned, the, the day Danish Foreign Minister leading that particular meeting, because we do believe it's important to highlight we have a special role in the Council as co-focal point together with Bahrain on conflict and hunger, which means that we have taken on ourselves a special responsibility to highlight the connections between conflict and hunger in the conflicts that we are working on in the Council.

Uh, Ukraine, um, again, you would have probably followed that since we entered on the Council a little more than a year and a half ago, it has been one of our main concerns. Not surprisingly, we're in the neighborhood. We're extremely concerned about this conflict, which has now been going on for more than 4 and a half years. It's something that we think it's important that the Council keeps discussing again to not have any conflicts become business as usual, but that for everyone to see that this is a horrible conflict taking place here. We've been really concerned the last 2, 3 months. I think we've been in the Council almost every week talking about the escalations in the attacks, which is why we've had several meetings, because the attacks just keep— the Russian attacks on Ukraine keep getting more and more brutal and more and more important in numbers, so to say. So we have, you know it much better than me, but almost every single night we have major attacks on Kyiv and other bigger cities of Ukraine. And of course, increasing number of civilian casualties. I believe that we heard that May and June were already the highest in numbers of civilian casualties so far in the conflict. And we haven't seen the final numbers for July yet, but I fear that that would be again beating that horrible record. So we have been pleading for more than a year for an immediate ceasefire, which Ukraine, of course, has been offering also for more than a year. It's quite clear to us that Russia does not want the ceasefire. So that's another reason for us to have meetings in the Council, so the rest of the Council members who have all at some point expressed the same wish get a chance to do that. And again, I've said this many times in the Council, but a just and lasting peace has to, of course, be in accordance with the basic principles of the Charter and respecting every state's sovereignty and territorial integrity. So we believe that a peace has to be comprehensive to be a lasting peace, and that would be the principle we keep working from and also the reason what we try to do this month in the Council. Lebanon, serious conversations. Yes, we all— our conversations are always serious in the Council, but of course we got the report from the Secretary-General about the post-UNIFIL options the 1st of June. We very much hope, because The end of the year is not so far from now, so we think the Council should discuss it, but we also have to, of course, take all this into consideration.
